questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: Amiloride differs from spironolactone in that:

options.label: B
options.text: Its diuretic action is more in the presence of conditions with elevated aldosterone levels.

options.label: C
options.text: It acts from the luminal membrane side of the distal tubular cells.

options.label: D
options.text: It can cause hypokalemia in long term use.

questions.answerText: It acts from the luminal membrane side of the distal tubular cells.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. It acts from the luminal membrane side of the distal tubular cells.

 

Amiloride acts from the luminal (urine) side of the distal tubular cells, where it inhibits epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), leading to decreased sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. On the other hand, spironolactone works intracellularly by binding to the mineralocorticoid receptor.

 

Other options

 

Option A. It has greater natriuretic action: Amiloride and spironolactone are both potassium-sparing diuretics, but spironolactone has more pronounced natriuretic effects when compared to amiloride. Therefore, this statement is incorrect.

 

Option B. Its diuretic action is more in the presence of conditions with elevated aldosterone levels: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist, meaning it specifically targets the mineralocorticoid receptor and inhibits the action of aldosterone. This makes it more effective in conditions with elevated aldosterone levels. Amiloride does not directly inhibit aldosterone; it blocks sodium channels in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting ducts. Therefore, this statement is incorrect.

 

Option D. It can cause hypokalemia on long term use: Both amiloride and spironolactone are potassium-sparing diuretics. Therefore, neither drug is likely to cause hypokalemia on long-term use; they are more likely to cause hyperkalemia if anything. This statement is incorrect.



ore, this statement is incorrect.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the clinic with recurrent episodes of renal colic. Laboratory tests and imaging confirm the presence of high-calcium renal stones. He has no other significant past medical history. What is the most useful diuretic in the treatment of his recurrent calcium stones?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Hydrochlorothiazide.

 

Hydrochlorothiazide is the diuretic of choice for preventing recurrent calcium stones. It acts in the distal convoluted tubule to decrease calcium excretion, thereby reducing the risk of calcium stone formation. It can also lower urinary calcium by enhancing calcium reabsorption in the kidney, which makes it less likely for calcium to form stones.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Furosemide: This loop diuretic works in the thick ascending limb of the Loop of Henle and increases calcium excretion. This would be counterproductive in the management of calcium renal stones and is not the ideal choice for this patient.

 

Option B. Spironolactone: This potassium-sparing diuretic is an aldosterone antagonist and has little to no effect on calcium reabsorption or excretion. It is not typically used for preventing calcium renal stones and is not suitable for this patient.

 

Option D. Acetazolamide: This diuretic is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and primarily used in the treatment of glaucoma or metabolic alkalosis. It can increase the pH of the urine, which might facilitate the formation of calcium phosphate stones. Therefore, it is not recommended for preventing calcium stones.



ore, it is not recommended for preventing calcium stones.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: Chlorthiazide and furosemide are members of different diuretic classes, in terms of mechanisms of action, but they share the ability to cause hypokalemia. Which of the following statements best describes the general mechanism by which these drugs cause their effects that lead to net renal loss of potassium?

options.label: B
options.text: Inhibiting Na+-K+-2C1– cotransport in the ascending limb of loop of Henle

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing the availability of Na+ in the distal tubular fluid to exchange with interstitial K+

questions.answerText: Increasing the availability of Na+ in the distal tubular fluid to exchange with interstitial K+
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Increasing the availability of Na+ in the distal tubular fluid to exchange with interstitial K+.

 

Both chlorthiazide and furosemide act by inhibiting sodium reabsorption at different parts of the nephron. Chlorthiazide acts at the distal convoluted tubule, while furosemide acts at the ascending limb of the Loop of Henle. As a result, they both increase the concentration of sodium in the distal tubular fluid. This increased sodium is then available for exchange with potassium, leading to enhanced potassium excretion and thereby increasing the risk of hypokalemia.

 

Option A. inhibiting proximal tubular K+ reabsorption: Neither chlorthiazide nor furosemide act primarily on the proximal tubule to inhibit potassium reabsorption.

 

Option B. Inhibiting Na+-K+-2Cl– cotransport in the ascending limb of loop of Henle: While it is true that furosemide works at this site, the mechanism of action does not directly involve potassium loss. Chlorthiazide does not act at this site at all.

 

Option D. Potentiating the action of aldosterone: Neither chlorthiazide nor furosemide potentiate the action of aldosterone. They can indirectly cause an increase in aldosterone due to volume depletion but do not potentiate its action directly.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: Postoperative vomiting is uncommon with this intravenous anaesthetic agent and patients can ambulate sooner than those who receive other anaesthetic agents:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Propofol.

 

Propofol is known for its rapid onset and short duration of action, which allows patients to recover more quickly and ambulate sooner compared to other anaesthetic agents. Additionally, propofol is associated with a lower incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV).

 

Option A. Ketamine: Although ketamine has rapid onset and recovery properties, it is more commonly associated with postoperative nausea and vomiting. It may also cause hallucinations and other psychological side effects, making it less desirable for quick ambulation.

 

Option B. Enflurane: Enflurane is an inhalational anaesthetic and generally has a slower onset and longer recovery time. It is also associated with a higher incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting compared to propofol.

 

Option D. Remifentanil: Remifentanil is an ultra-short-acting opioid analgesic, not a primary anaesthetic agent. While it may be used in conjunction with other anaesthetics, by itself it does not provide the desired anaesthetic effects. Additionally, opioids like remifentanil can be associated with postoperative nausea and vomiting.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is scheduled for emergency surgery due to acute appendicitis. He has no significant past medical history, but his medical team is concerned about the use of succinylcholine as a neuromuscular blocking agent for intubation. Which of the following statements about succinylcholine is true?

options.label: B
options.text: It has a long duration of action.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the drug of choice in non-traumatic rhabdomyolysis.

options.label: D
options.text: It is useful in patients with spinal cord injuries with paraplegia.

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. It may induce life-threatening hyperkalemia.

 

Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that can potentially induce life-threatening hyperkalemia, especially in patients with pre-existing hyperkalemia, burns, or certain neuromuscular disorders. This risk is a critical consideration when choosing a neuromuscular blocker for intubation or surgery.

 

Other options:

 

Option B. It has a long duration of action: Succinylcholine has a very short duration of action, usually lasting only a few minutes. This makes it ideal for short procedures but contradicts this statement.

 

Option C. It is the drug of choice in non-traumatic rhabdomyolysis: Succinylcholine is contraindicated in cases of rhabdomyolysis, as it may exacerbate hyperkalemia and worsen the condition.

 

Option D. It is useful in patients with spinal cord injuries with paraplegia: Succinylcholine is generally avoided in patients with spinal cord injuries due to the risk of hyperkalemia.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is scheduled for a minor surgical procedure. She has a history of chronic pain and is looking for an anaesthetic that provides both analgesia and amnesia but allows her to maintain some level of consciousness. Which anaesthetic is known for producing “dissociative anaesthesia”?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Ketamine.

 

Ketamine is known for producing a state of "dissociative anaesthesia," which provides analgesia, amnesia, and altered perception while maintaining some level of consciousness. This characteristic makes it useful in certain types of procedures and in patients with chronic pain issues.

 

Option A. Fentanyl: Fentanyl is a powerful opioid analgesic but does not produce dissociative anaesthesia. It provides strong analgesia but not the altered perception or amnesia that is associated with dissociative anaesthesia.

 

Option B. Propofol: Propofol is an intravenous anaesthetic agent used for induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia. It does not produce dissociative anaesthesia but rather causes sedation and loss of consciousness.

 

Option D. Sevoflurane: Sevoflurane is an inhalational anaesthetic and is not known for producing dissociative anaesthesia. It is generally used for induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: Which of the following beta 2 agonists is given by inhalation, and is suitable for both terminating acute asthma attacks as well as for prophylaxis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Formoterol.

 

Formoterol is a long-acting beta-2 agonist that has a rapid onset of action, making it suitable for both acute relief and long-term control of asthma symptoms. Unlike other long-acting beta-2 agonists like salmeterol, formoterol's quick onset allows it to be used for terminating acute asthma attacks as well as for prophylaxis.

 

Option A. Terbutaline: This is a short-acting beta-2 agonist primarily used for relief of acute asthma symptoms but generally not used for long-term control or prophylaxis.

 

Option B. Salbutamol: This short-acting beta-2 agonist is effective for terminating acute asthma attacks but is generally not used for long-term prophylaxis alone.

 

Option D. Salmeterol: Salmeterol is a long-acting beta-2 agonist used for long-term control of asthma symptoms, typically in combination with an inhaled corticosteroid. However, it is not suitable for terminating acute asthma attacks due to its slower onset of action.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of carpel tunnel syndrome is scheduled for a peripheral nerve block procedure. The anaesthesiologist is considering adding epinephrine to the lignocaine solution for the nerve block. What will be the effect of adding epinephrine to lignocaine in this situation?

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the duration of action of the local anaesthetic.

options.label: C
options.text: Accelerate the onset of local anaesthesia.

questions.answerText: Increase the duration of action of the local anaesthetic.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Increase the duration of action of the local anaesthetic.

 

Adding epinephrine to lignocaine serves to vasoconstrict the blood vessels at the site of injection, reducing systemic absorption of the anaesthetic. This has the effect of prolonging the duration of action of the local anaesthetic at the site of injection.

 

Option A. increase risk of convulsions: Adding epinephrine does not generally increase the risk of convulsions. Its vasoconstrictive effect may decrease the systemic absorption of the local anaesthetic, potentially reducing the risk of systemic toxicity and convulsions.

 

Option C. Accelerate the onset of local anaesthesia: This statement is incorrect. Adding epinephrine does not accelerate the onset of local anaesthesia; rather, it prolongs the duration of the anaesthetic effect.

 

Option D. both (a) and (b): As mentioned, adding epinephrine does not generally increase the risk of convulsions, making this option incorrect.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with acute liver and renal failure. Her lab reports show a serum bilirubin level of 8 mg/dl and a serum creatinine level of 4 mg/dl. She requires muscle relaxation for mechanical ventilation. What would be the muscle relaxant of choice in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Atracurium.

 

Atracurium is metabolized through Hoffman elimination, which is independent of hepatic and renal function. Therefore, it is a suitable choice for patients with liver and kidney dysfunction.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Pancuronium: This muscle relaxant undergoes hepatic metabolism and renal excretion, making it less suitable for patients with liver and kidney dysfunction.

 

Option B. Mivacurium: Mivacurium is metabolized by plasma cholinesterase and undergoes renal excretion. Liver disease can result in decreased cholinesterase activity, which would prolong the duration of action of mivacurium.

 

Option D. d-Tubocurarine: This muscle relaxant is primarily excreted by the kidneys, and thus is not suitable for patients with renal failure.



ore, it is a suitable choice for patients with liver and kidney dysfunction.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: We have a patient with heart failure, unacceptably low cardiac output, and intense reflex-mediated sympathetic activation of the peripheral vasculature that is attempting to keep vital organ perfusion pressure sufficiently high. The patient is edematous, and has ascites, because of the poor cardiac function and renal compensations for it. Which one of the following drugs should be avoided in this patient because it is most likely to compromise function of the already failing heart by increasing intravascular volume?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Mannitol.

 

Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that works by increasing the osmolarity of the glomerular filtrate. This draws water out of cells and into the vascular space, increasing intravascular volume. In a patient with heart failure and low cardiac output, an increase in intravascular volume can exacerbate the existing cardiac failure and should be avoided.

 

Option A. Amiloride: This potassium-sparing diuretic works in the distal tubules and collecting ducts and would not significantly increase intravascular volume in a way that would compromise heart function in the scenario described.

 

Option B. Hydrochlorothiazide: This thiazide diuretic would likely help to decrease intravascular volume by promoting sodium and water excretion. While it could potentially affect electrolytes and cardiac rhythm, it wouldn't directly compromise cardiac function by increasing intravascular volume.

 

Option D. Spironolactone: Like amiloride, spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic that works on the aldosterone-sensitive cells in the distal tubule and collecting duct. It would not significantly increase intravascular volume in a manner that would be contraindicated in the patient described.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: One of your clinic patients is being treated with spironolactone. Which of the following statements best describes the property of this drug?

options.label: A
options.text: Inhibits Na+ reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule of the nephron.

options.label: C
options.text: Is a rational choice for a patient with an adrenal cortical tumor.

options.label: D
options.text: Is more efficacious than hydrochlorothiazide in all patients who receive the drug.

questions.answerText: Is a rational choice for a patient with an adrenal cortical tumor.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Is a rational choice for a patient with an adrenal cortical tumor

 

Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic that acts as an aldosterone antagonist. It is often used in the treatment of conditions where aldosterone secretion is abnormally high, such as in patients with adrenal cortical tumors.

 

Option A. Inhibits Na+ reabsorption in the proximal renal tubule of the nephron: Spironolactone does not act on the proximal renal tubule. Its site of action is the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct where it antagonizes the action of aldosterone.

 

Option B. interferes with aldosterone synthesis: Spironolactone does not interfere with aldosterone synthesis; it antagonizes the action of aldosterone at its receptor.

 

Option D. is more efficacious than hydrochlorothiazide in all patients who receive the drug: The efficacy of spironolactone compared to hydrochlorothiazide would depend on the underlying condition being treated and cannot be universally stated as more efficacious for all patients.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A 60-year-old male with a history of hypertension has been on long-term therapy with lisinopril. Despite medication, his blood pressure remains poorly controlled. His physician decides to add triamterene to his medication regimen. What is the most likely outcome of combining these two drugs?

options.label: A
options.text: Better BP control, but with a risk of hyperkalemia

options.label: B
options.text: Cardiac depression, because both drugs directly depress the heart

options.label: C
options.text: Cough that may be severe, even though there was no cough with lisinopril alone

options.label: D
options.text: Hypernatremia, because ACE inhibitors counteract triamterene’s natriuretic effect

questions.answerText: Better BP control, but with a risk of hyperkalemia
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Better BP control, but with a risk of hyperkalemia.

 

Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor that reduces blood pressure partly by blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Triamterene is a potassium-sparing diuretic that inhibits the reabsorption of sodium ions in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions. When combined, both drugs can effectively lower blood pressure. However, because both drugs have potassium-sparing effects (lisinopril can increase potassium levels by reducing aldosterone secretion), there is an increased risk of hyperkalemia.

 

Option B. Cardiac depression, because both drugs directly depress the heart: Neither lisinopril nor triamterene directly depress the heart, making this statement incorrect.

 

Option C. Cough that may be severe, even though there was no cough with lisinopril alone: Cough is a well-known side effect of ACE inhibitors like lisinopril but is not directly related to the addition of triamterene.

 

Option D. Hypernatremia, because ACE inhibitors counteract triamterene’s natriuretic effect: Both drugs have the potential to reduce sodium levels rather than increase them. ACE inhibitors can decrease aldosterone secretion, and triamterene promotes natriuresis. This makes hypernatremia unlikely.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: Your patient, who lives in Delhi, is planning a vacation that includes a short hike to the top of Mount Everest (altitude approx. 29,000 feet above sea level). You’re concerned about “altitude sickness.” He has no other significant medical conditions and takes no other drugs that would interact with the drug you will prescribe for his trip. Which of the following drugs would you recommend that this adventurer start taking before his trek, and continue until he returns to an altitude much closer to sea level?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Acetazolamide.

 

Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that can be used prophylactically to prevent symptoms of acute mountain sickness, commonly known as "altitude sickness." It promotes diuresis and metabolic acidosis, thereby helping the body acclimate to high altitudes more quickly.

 

Option B. Amiloride: This is a potassium-sparing diuretic primarily used to treat conditions like hypertension and edema and has no role in preventing altitude sickness.

 

Option C. Furosemide: This is a loop diuretic, and while it might seem tempting to think that a diuretic could help avoid fluid retention at high altitudes, it's not recommended for this indication.

 

Option D. Triamterene: Like amiloride, triamterene is a potassium-sparing diuretic that is not used for preventing altitude sickness.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A young man having pheochromocytoma has BP of 188/92 mm Hg and a hematocrit of around 50%. Pulmonary function tests and renal functions are normal. His catecholamines are elevated. Which of the following drugs should not be included in the anesthesia protocol?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Halothane.

 

Halothane is a volatile anesthetic that is generally contraindicated in cases of pheochromocytoma due to its propensity to sensitize the myocardium to catecholamines. In a patient with pheochromocytoma, who already has elevated catecholamine levels, this can precipitate cardiac arrhythmias and other complications.

 

Option A. Desflurane: Desflurane is considered a safer volatile anesthetic in pheochromocytoma cases compared to halothane because it does not sensitize the myocardium to catecholamines to the same extent.

 

Option B. Fentanyl: This opioid analgesic is generally safe to use in patients with pheochromocytoma. It does not release catecholamines and therefore is not contraindicated.

 

Option D. Midazolam: This benzodiazepine can be used for its anxiolytic and amnesic properties and is not contraindicated in pheochromocytoma.



ore is not contraindicated.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true of local anaesthetics?

options.label: A
options.text: The local anaesthetic is required in the unionized form for penetrating the neuronal membrane.

options.label: B
options.text: The local anaesthetic approaches its receptor only from the intraneuronal face of the Na+ channel.

options.label: C
options.text: The local anaesthetic binds to its receptor mainly when the Na+ channel is in the resting state.

options.label: D
options.text: The local anaesthetic combines with its receptor in the ionized cationic form.

questions.answerText: The local anaesthetic binds to its receptor mainly when the Na+ channel is in the resting state.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. The local anaesthetic binds to its receptor mainly when the Na+ channel is in the resting state.

 

Local anaesthetics primarily bind to their sodium channel receptor when the channel is in the activated or inactivated state, not the resting state. This is the basis for their use-dependent or "frequency-dependent" blockade, where the blockade is more effective with higher rates of neuronal firing.

 

Option A. True. The local anaesthetic is more lipophilic in its unionized form, which allows it to penetrate the hydrophobic cellular membrane more easily.

 

Option B. True. The local anaesthetic mainly approaches its receptor from the intraneuronal face of the Na+ channel, gaining access through the open channel during depolarization.

 

Option D. True. Once inside the neuron, the local anaesthetic will ionize in the more acidic intracellular environment and bind to the sodium channel in its ionized, cationic form.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A patient came to emergency with pus on the tip of the finger. You want to drain the pus and require a local anaesthetic. The history of the patient reveals that he is allergic to chlorprocaine. Which of the following local anaesthetics will be safe in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Lignocaine without adrenaline.

 

In a patient with a history of allergy to chlorprocaine, it is advisable to avoid ester-type local anaesthetics like tetracaine. Chlorprocaine and tetracaine both belong to the ester class of local anaesthetics, and cross-reactivity can occur. Lignocaine (also known as lidocaine) is an amide-type local anaesthetic, and is generally considered safer in a patient with known ester-type local anaesthetic allergy.

 

Option A and B. Tetracaine with or without adrenaline: Tetracaine is an ester-type local anaesthetic. Patients allergic to one ester-type local anaesthetic are at risk of being allergic to other esters, so both these options would be unsafe.

 

Option C. Lignocaine with adrenaline: Lignocaine is generally safe as it is an amide-type local anaesthetic. However, the addition of adrenaline (epinephrine) can cause issues in areas with end arteries like the fingers, nose, and penis due to the vasoconstrictive effect, so it should be avoided for this procedure.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A patient has very high serum uric acid levels, has had two acute gout attacks, and is at imminent risk of developing acute uric acid nephropathy. We will treat the patient with proper anti-inflammatory drugs and other agents but feel that reducing solubility of uric acid in the urine, by raising urine pH, might help stave-off the development of renal problems. Which of the following drugs produce this desired renal effect without appreciably increasing systemic risks of the hyperuricemia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Acetazolamide.

 

Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that increases the excretion of bicarbonate, thereby alkalizing the urine. Alkaline urine helps increase the solubility of uric acid, reducing the risk of acute uric acid nephropathy. It does not have a major impact on systemic uric acid levels.

 

Option B. Vasopressin: This is an antidiuretic hormone that primarily acts on the renal collecting duct to increase water reabsorption. It does not have a significant impact on urine pH or uric acid solubility.

 

Option C. Furosemide: This loop diuretic can increase uric acid levels and may exacerbate gout. Moreover, it does not alkalize the urine to improve uric acid solubility.

 

Option D. Hydrochlorothiazide: This thiazide diuretic is known to increase serum uric acid levels and does not alkalize the urine. Therefore, it is not a good choice in this context.



ore, it is not a good choice in this context.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A patient with bronchial asthma has been on theophylline therapy. After the addition of a new medication to his regimen, he starts exhibiting symptoms of theophylline toxicity. Which of the following drugs was most likely added to his regimen?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Erythromycin.

 

Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic known to inhibit cytochrome P450 enzymes, which are responsible for the metabolism of many drugs, including theophylline. Inhibiting these enzymes increases the plasma levels of theophylline, potentially leading to toxicity.

 

Option B. Phenytoin: Phenytoin is an antiepileptic drug that is a cytochrome P450 enzyme inducer, rather than an inhibitor. It would be more likely to reduce the levels of theophylline, not increase them.

 

Option C. Griseofulvin: This antifungal medication is not known for significant interactions with theophylline metabolism.

 

Option D. Rifampicin: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of cytochrome P450 enzymes. Like phenytoin, it would decrease the levels of theophylline, not increase them.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A patient with COPD was given intravenous aminophylline therapy following which the patient developed diuresis. This is due to action on which effector?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Adenosine receptors.

 

Aminophylline is a theophylline derivative that acts as an adenosine receptor antagonist. Blocking adenosine receptors can lead to diuresis, along with other actions such as bronchodilation. Adenosine typically has an anti-diuretic action on the kidneys; therefore, its blockade would promote diuresis.

 

Option B. Beta 2 adrenergic receptors: Aminophylline does not act on beta 2 adrenergic receptors. Moreover, beta 2 receptors are involved in causing bronchodilation and not diuresis.

 

Option C. IL-10: Interleukin 10 (IL-10) is an anti-inflammatory cytokine. Aminophylline's diuretic effects are not associated with IL-10.

 

Option D. Histone deacetylase: Aminophylline is not known to work via histone deacetylases for its diuretic effects.



ore, its blockade would promote diuresis.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 012-T-20 Pharmacology Test-10 (Kidney, Respiratory System & Anaesthesia) - 18-09-2023 - 2023-09-18
questions.stem: A young female presented to hospital for treatment of gout. She did not talk about pre-existing history of asthma. The intern gave aspirin after which acute attack of asthma was precipitated. Which of the following is the likely cause of the bronchoconstriction in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Augmentation of LOX pathway.

 

In aspirin-sensitive asthma, the inhibition of the cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway by aspirin leads to a shunting of arachidonic acid metabolism towards the lipoxygenase (LOX) pathway. This results in the production of leukotrienes, potent bronchoconstrictors that can precipitate an asthma attack.

 

Option A. Blockade of COX pathway: While it's true that aspirin blocks the COX pathway, it is the shunting to the LOX pathway that results in bronchoconstriction.

 

Option B. PG mediated bronchoconstriction: Aspirin inhibits prostaglandin (PG) synthesis by blocking the COX pathway, thus this is not the likely cause of bronchoconstriction.

 

Option D. Release of histamine: Aspirin-induced bronchoconstriction in asthma is not primarily mediated by histamine release.
